One thing to do is to try different starting values.

However, I think this is a weird looking model. You've got a lot of  variables, and very few covariances. (I didn't spend the time to draw out the path diagram, but if you did, it would be helpful).

Some of your variances are small - the usual advice is to make sure that the variances of your variables are within an order of magnitude of one another, or you run into precision estimates.

Finally, you have some negative variances - variances can't be negative, so whether you have fit indices or not, you know that this model is wrong.

Hope that helps,

jeremy

Hello Keith,

Thank you for your answer. I've never tried to specify starting values before, but you've given me quite the array of strategies to look into :)

I will also try to figure why I am getting negative variances in the first place

Thank you!

Federica

Il giorno sabato 29 febbraio 2020 14:00:54 UTC, Nickname ha scritto:
> Federica,
>   This kind of issue received a lot of attention for simpler SEM models in the early days of SEM.  Here are some general strategies.
>
> 1. Try using previous research to choose better start values.
> 2. Try fitting the model from a variety of different start values (this was automated in Mx).
> 3. Try extending the number of iterations, or refitting the model using the non-converged estimates as start values.
> 4. Try fitting a simplified model to obtain reasonable start values for some of the parameters and then use those to fit the full model.
> 5. Try to intuit potential problems from unusual or out-of-bounds values among the non-converged parameter estimates.
>
>   It may be that in fitting simplified submodels, you would also discover parameters such as yours that can be fixed to zero.  Negative variances are nonsensical, and thus always indicate a problem somewhere in the model.  Nothing can vary less than a constant.
>
> Keith
> ------------------------

> John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
> http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'd like to model the two models in the figure (among others) and don't get further, so hopefully someone has an idea for me. All data stems from an experimental design, thus it is not possible to change X or Z. For Y, I also have continuous versions of the DV but in simpler models, they did not work as good as the binary DVs. Also, I checked and the problem was not fixed by changing from binary to continuous DV.

Did it work at all?
Yes it did - I provided the code below. But I tried replicating the results of Model 1 using SPSS PROCESS macro and the lavaan output does not show the same results.
Therefore, I am doubting, whether the results of Model 2 are at all correct but I cannot model this in the PROCESS macro because it simply can't do that.

What I guess what the problem is?
A combination of dichotomous IV, moderator and DV as well as the combination of using regression and logistic regression in the same model. The output suggests that the effects are driven by the moderator and not by the interaction as expected and shown using SPSS PROCESS macro.
Specifically, it does not help neither to declare the binary variables as ordered or to declare the binary variables as factors before calculating the interaction. Because then, lavaan simply cannot work with them anymore. Hence, I am not sure, whether it is at all possible to model this with lavaan and whether I should instead switch to MPlus for this.

Code for Model 1:
model_INFmodmed <-  '
# Equations
Y ~ con2*1 + cdash*X + b*M2_INF
M2_INF ~ con1*1 + a1*X + a2*Z + az*XZ

# indirect and total effects on Z=0
ab0 := a1*b
total0 := ab0 + cdash

#indirect and total effects on Z=1
ab1 := (a1+az)*b
total1 := ab1 + cdash

# Index of moderated mediation
index := ab0 - ab1
          '
fit_INFmodmed <- sem(model_INFmodmed, data = Data)
summary(fit_INFmodmed)

Code for Model 2:
model_seqmodmed <- '
# Equations
Y ~ con1*1 + cdash*X + d*M2_INF
M1_GA ~ con2*1 + a*X
M2_INF ~ con3*1 + b1*M1_GA + b2*Z + bz*M1_GA:Z

# indirect and total effects on Z=0
ab0 := a*b1
total0 := ab0 + cdash

#indirect and total effects on Z=1
ab1 := a*(b1+bz)
total1 := ab1 + cdash

# Index of moderated mediation
index := ab0 - ab1
          '
fit_seqmodmed <- sem(model_seqmodmed, data = Data)
summary(fit_seqmodmed)

I hope that someone has an idea, I ran out of ideas to solve this. Thanks a lot in advance!

messages.body_plain:
First of all, thank you very much for a very detailed and informative response.

We have consulted the literature you mention, and some other papers discussing the subject and feel we have a much better grasp of what's going on.

On Thursday, February 27, 2020 at 10:40:45 PM UTC+1, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > 1) Since we are using ordinal indicators, we are using the WLSMW estimator. We have found in the literature that this requires a sample size between 200 and 500. But how does this work with multigroups structure? Does it mean that we would need 500 participants per group?
>
> For asymptotic behaviors to kick in, yes, but the N required also depends on the size of your model and reliability of your indicators.  Models that estimate more parameters (which are closer to zero in the population) require more data for stability.

Okay, thanks for the clarification.

>
>
> > 2) Some pooled estimates have infinite degrees of freedom, is this a problem, and what does it mean? How can p vales even be calculated with infinite degrees of freedom?
>
> A t distribution with infinite df is the normal distribution.  The semTools package just rounds df > 9999 to Inf to prevent ugly displays (and because there is no practical difference between t and z statistics.

Makes sense, we just figured calculation with anything being Inf would be problematic.

>
> > 3) How exactly are standardized solutions pooled across imputations?
>
> The same way as for complete data, but using pooled unstandardized estimates, which are standardized using pooled saturated-model estimates.
>
>
> > In our case factor loadings, for example, have the same values for standardized and non-standardized parameter estimates. This is not the case when evaluating models on individual imputed datasets.
>
> Really?  If you are using parameterization="delta" and std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, you should expect them to be the same because they are by definition.  If you think something is amiss, please provide a reproducible example.

No, we are using theta, but I couldn't come up with a reproducible example, I think it could be down to the way the latents were scaled, which differed between cfa and cfa.mi cases, will revisit this.

>

messages.subject: confusion about regression operation in CFA
messages.subject_clean: confusion about regression operation in CFA
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys!

I'm now developing a new measurement and want to test its correlation to ability latents in an established model from literature.

The behavioral model is a bi-factor CFA model which has a general factor g, and nested factors vis, cry, spd and mem. All the factors are orthogonal otherwise the model will not converge.

My confusion raises when I keep the behavior model and regress my measurement, called HB, on to these latents. If I do it separately, means regress only one factor to HB in one model, the estimations are not significant.

Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
  g ~
    HB1               0.023    0.037    0.634    0.526    0.023    0.023

Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
  spd ~
    HB               0.054    0.039    1.391    0.164    0.054    0.054

When I simultaneously regress all the factors on HB, the results can be significant:

Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
  g ~
    HB1              -0.278    0.119   -2.342    0.019   -0.268   -0.267
  vis ~
    HB1               0.366    0.197    1.857    0.063    0.344    0.343
  cry ~
    HB1               0.707    0.252    2.808    0.005    0.577    0.577
  spd ~
    HB1               0.178    0.063    2.823    0.005    0.176    0.175
  mem ~
    HB1               0.293    0.135    2.175    0.030    0.281    0.281

But this result is also problematic because all the task measurements I used to construct the latents are positively correlated so the negative estimation of g appears to be weird.

I'm wondering what I did wrong because the two causes are supposed to be similar. If I did not make mistakes which result should I trust?

I appreciate all your valuable suggestions!

Bests regard.

messages.subject_clean: confusion about regression operation in CFA
messages.body_plain:
When you use HB1 to predict just one dependent, the other dependents are in the model, yes? But with the potential paths from HB1 constrained to 0? It could be that misspecification (forcing paths to 0 that should not be 0) is biasing the individual coefficient estimates. If this is correct, then you should be seeing evidence of the lack of fit in the fit indices and modification indices for the more limited models. The estimation method is trying to optimize fit overall. In the more limited models, it may be that keeping an estimated path close to 0 minimizes the overall lack of fit when other paths are being forced to 0.

messages.subject: Re: confusion about regression operation in CFA
messages.subject_clean: confusion about regression operation in CFA
messages.body_plain:
Maybe the results is caused by your "all factors orthogonal" model not being best for the data. You indicated that you forced all factors to be orthogonal in order to achieve identification. But that was before adding HB1 as a common predictor, yes? Having this extra (observed?) variable in the model could change the identification situation. Since HB1 predicts all of the other factors in the model, it acts a little bit like a common factor itself, and so now you may have some lack of fit because this almost-common factor model does not match up with the data. Try relaxing the orthogonality constraint among the group factors--allow residual covariance among them--while leaving the constraints in place between the general factor and the group factors. See if that makes the surprising result go away.

messages.subject: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation
messages.subject_clean: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone!

I am currently trying to fit a model with 46 items, however, I have only 150 participants per group (3 groups). When fitting the model to the separate groups, the CFI value was not acceptable <.90. I'd like to know if it was due to insufficient sample size. I was suggested to run a simulation study.

I found the simsem package, which in Example 7 (analyzing real data and then run monte carlo simulation https://github.com/simsem/simsem/wiki/Example-7:-Analyzing-Real-Data-and-then-Run-Monte-Carlo-Simulation), it said, "As a benefit, this procedure will yield a distribution of fit indices from simulated data when the hypothesized model is correct. This distribution can compare with the result of the real data. This procedure is called a Monte Carlo approach for model evaluation."

I have a few questions about it:
1) does it mean that if the fit indices from the real sample (e.g. CFI) is greater than the alpha = 0.05 cufoff value from the the simulations, then the hypothesized model can be accepted?
2) can I do the simulations with a bigger sample size than the original n? For example, the fit indices distribution with n=500 per group? Does it make sense?
3) Is there any emperical or methodological literature regarding this approach? From reading the threads, I was directed to a paper by Preacher and Selig (2012) which, if I understood correctly, advocated the monte carlo approach to evaluate indirect effects confidence intervals. Is that the same thing as evaluating model fits?
4) are there any guidelines in terms of the allowed misspecifications in the simulations? e.g., the crossloadings specified in the example were between -0.2 and 0.2.
5) The above questions are all about fitting the hypothesized model to a single group, will this approach also work for multiple-group invariance testing? Is there also a need to specify misspecifications for the multiple group simulations?

I am just recently looking at simulations/bootstrap in sem. I sincerely apologize if these questions seem too naive. Thank you very much in advance!

Erin

messages.subject: Re: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation
messages.subject_clean: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation
messages.body_plain:
Erin,
  I am not a statistician but here is my take on your questions.

 1) does it mean that if the fit indices from the real sample (e.g. CFI) is greater than the alpha = 0.05 cufoff value from the the simulations, then the hypothesized model can be accepted?

  As in any other situation, decisions about fit and model acceptance should never be made on the basis of one number, not even compared to a reference distribution.  Consider a variety of indices, do not ignore chi-square, and also look at local fit information such as estimates and residuals.  If your CFI is in the rejection region, it means that it is unlikely to have been generated if the model were correct.  If the CFI falls outside the rejection region, between the tails, then you cannot rule out your model, but the same could likely be said for many rival hypotheses as well.

> 2) can I do the simulations with a bigger sample size than the original n? For example, the fit indices distribution with n=500 per group? Does it make sense?

This will tell you what you would expect if you ran the study with more cases and the model used to simulate the data were correct.

> 3) Is there any emperical or methodological literature regarding this approach? From reading the threads, I was directed to a paper by Preacher and Selig (2012) which, if I understood correctly, advocated the monte carlo approach to evaluate indirect effects confidence intervals. Is that the same thing as evaluating model fits?

They are analogous, allowing for the fact that the tests are reversed.  For a parameter, the null hypothesis is zero.  For fit, the analog to a null hypothesis is perfect fit.

> 4) are there any guidelines in terms of the allowed misspecifications in the simulations? e.g., the crossloadings specified in the example were between -0.2 and 0.2.

The simulation assumes that the simulated model is correctly specified.  You can explore the impact of misspecification with further simulations (e.g., with corss-loadings) but these results are specific to the pattern of misspecification that you simulate.

> 5) The above questions are all about fitting the hypothesized model to a single group, will this approach also work for multiple-group invariance testing? Is there also a need to specify misspecifications for the multiple group simulations?
>

I do not see anything that would prevent you from trying this.  However, there is no magic here.  The more complex the model, the more you are pressing the limits of your data.  My guess is that your simulations will confirm that it is very hard to answer your questions based on your data.  You might explore using a Bayesian approach to compensate for lack of data by making stronger explicit assumptions.  However, there is really no getting around the limited size of your data set except by collecting more data.  The Bayesian approach would just give you more flexibility in the balance that you choose between  paying for the small sample in the currency of low power and in the currency of strong assumptions.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to fit a sem model and include socioeconomic factors (income, educational attainment). I've tried including these variables in a latent variable 'ses' as well as using them as exogenous variables in the regression model. In both cases, the model produces the following warning:

Warning message:
In pc_cor_TS(fit.y1 = UNI[[i]], fit.y2 = UNI[[j]], method = optim.method,  :
  no convergence

The sample size is n=36015. When I remove all of the socioeconomic factors, the model runs, but adding any one individually to the model produces an error. The simplest model (model 1), without socioeconomic factors, converges and has a good fit. But I want to include these other factors as control variables. Model 3 specifies these factors, and it's the one that don't run. Here's my code:

model1<- "
#Measurement part of model
polpart =~ NA*wrkprty + wrkorg + contplt + sgnptit + pbldmn + bctprd
poltrust =~ NA*trstprl + trstplt + trstprt

#Structural part of model
polpart ~ poltrust + female + agea

polpart~~1*polpart
poltrust~~1*poltrust
"

m1fit<-sem(model=model1, data=ess)

model3<- "
#Measurement part of model
polpart =~ NA*wrkprty + wrkorg + contplt + sgnptit + pbldmn + bctprd
poltrust =~ NA*trstprl + trstplt + trstprt
ses =~ NA*eisced + hinctnta + hincfel

#Structural part of model
polpart ~ poltrust + female + agea + ses

polpart~~1*polpart
poltrust~~1*poltrust
ses~~1*ses
"
m3fit<-sem(model=model3, data=ess)

I'm able to view the model fit using summary(), but the standardized coefficients (std.all) aren't available for model 3. If you have any suggestions for how to make my model converge, please let me know! Thank you :)

On 3/12/20 12:22 PM, Aiden wrote:
> However, for the second model where all the error terms were allowed to
> covary, I recevied a warning from lavaan.
>
> Warning message:
> In lav_model_hessian(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats =
> lavsamplestats,  :
>    lavaan WARNING: Hessian is not fully symmetric. Max diff =
> 4.84723343639228e-06
>
> Could someone please help to explain what this mean?

This a numerical issue that occurs when computing the Hessian of the
free parameters. I recently added a check to verify if the Hessian is
symmetric (as needed), and this check is currently somewhat too
sensitive. It is usually triggered when some observed variances are much
larger than others. But since in your case, the 'difference' is so tiny,
it has no effect. You can safely ignore it.

The 'check' is now more robust in the dev version of lavaan.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation
messages.subject_clean: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Keith,

Thank you very much for your comprehensive reply! I will have to digest them first before I could raise any follow-up questions (I am sure there will be plenty).

Thank you again for your time and effort!

Best,

Erin

On Thursday, 12 March 2020 03:01:20 UTC+13, Nickname wrote:
> Erin,
>   I am not a statistician but here is my take on your questions.
>
>  1) does it mean that if the fit indices from the real sample (e.g. CFI) is greater than the alpha = 0.05 cufoff value from the the simulations, then the hypothesized model can be accepted?
>
>   As in any other situation, decisions about fit and model acceptance should never be made on the basis of one number, not even compared to a reference distribution.  Consider a variety of indices, do not ignore chi-square, and also look at local fit information such as estimates and residuals.  If your CFI is in the rejection region, it means that it is unlikely to have been generated if the model were correct.  If the CFI falls outside the rejection region, between the tails, then you cannot rule out your model, but the same could likely be said for many rival hypotheses as well.
>
>
> > 2) can I do the simulations with a bigger sample size than the original n? For example, the fit indices distribution with n=500 per group? Does it make sense?
>
>
> This will tell you what you would expect if you ran the study with more cases and the model used to simulate the data were correct.
>
>
> > 3) Is there any emperical or methodological literature regarding this approach? From reading the threads, I was directed to a paper by Preacher and Selig (2012) which, if I understood correctly, advocated the monte carlo approach to evaluate indirect effects confidence intervals. Is that the same thing as evaluating model fits?
>
> They are analogous, allowing for the fact that the tests are reversed.  For a parameter, the null hypothesis is zero.  For fit, the analog to a null hypothesis is perfect fit.
>
>
> > 4) are there any guidelines in terms of the allowed misspecifications in the simulations? e.g., the crossloadings specified in the example were between -0.2 and 0.2.
>
> The simulation assumes that the simulated model is correctly specified.  You can explore the impact of misspecification with further simulations (e.g., with corss-loadings) but these results are specific to the pattern of misspecification that you simulate.
>
>
> > 5) The above questions are all about fitting the hypothesized model to a single group, will this approach also work for multiple-group invariance testing? Is there also a need to specify misspecifications for the multiple group simulations?
> >
>
> I do not see anything that would prevent you from trying this.  However, there is no magic here.  The more complex the model, the more you are pressing the limits of your data.  My guess is that your simulations will confirm that it is very hard to answer your questions based on your data.  You might explore using a Bayesian approach to compensate for lack of data by making stronger explicit assumptions.  However, there is really no getting around the limited size of your data set except by collecting more data.  The Bayesian approach would just give you more flexibility in the balance that you choose between  paying for the small sample in the currency of low power and in the currency of strong assumptions.
>
> Keith
> ------------------------
> Keith A. Markus
> John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
> http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
> Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
> http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
>

messages.subject: Autoregressive errors in multilevel, multigroup CFA
messages.subject_clean: Autoregressive errors in multilevel, multigroup CFA
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Does anyone know if the inclusion of autoregressive errors in a multilevel, multigroup CFA is implemented in lavaan? And if yes, are you aware of any documentation on how to fit this kind of model? I have been searching online but have not found anything yet. I am also new to this topic.

Our data is structured in the following way: We have several items measuring mood at multiple time points (~80) nested in persons (~150). Persons are divided in groups and we would like to test for measurement invariance of the factor structures across these groups. Mood ratings closer in time are expected to be more similar, so an autoregressive error structure would be most appropriate. There are also relatively many missing time points.

Any help would be much appreciated!

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: Getting R Squared in Lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Getting R Squared in Lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kimberly,

R^2 are specific to "regression equations". Based on the information you provided it appears that your model is made up of four "regressions" and the values you see there are the respective r^2. To the best of my knowledge, there is no such thing as overall R^2 for the whole model in CFA/SEM. It exists only if you have just one "regression equation" in your whole model, the majority of SEM models (for example in your case) are composed of numerous "regression equations".

Pita

messages.subject: Re: CFA difference in results between R and Mplus
messages.subject_clean: CFA difference in results between R and Mplus
messages.body_plain:
When using ordered items, lavaan will present more differences from Mplus. Lavaan can tell you which equations are being use to estimate these models, while Mplus differed even when they say (in their technical papers) that they use the same equations.
A while back Yves stop trying to match the Mplus output, as it becomes a tedious bactracking process of which changes Mplus is making to the original equations. And in lavaan we know exactly which equations are being used, so we are more confident on this\.
Mplus is famous for hidding parts of their process, to keep their software hard to replicate. But this ends in issues like this, as we are not clear what is going on under the hood

messages.subject: Re: Getting R Squared in Lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Getting R Squared in Lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hayduk (1996, ch. 6) attributed a Coefficient of Determination for an entire model to the LISREL 7 manual and Sorbom (1989).  It was calculated as follows.

1 - (|psi| / |Cov(eta)|)

Where psi is the matrix of disturbance variances, Cov(eta) is the covariance matrix of endogenous latent variables, and |x| is the determinant of x.  Hayduk criticized this measure for its sensitivity to the covariances between the latent variables.

To the best of my knowledge, the criticism stuck, and standard practice today is to inspect the individual R^2 values for each equation rather than attempt to summarize them across the entire model.  This is in keeping the Kline's emphasis on the importance of evaluating local fit.

However, you could compute this quantity by (a) extracting the two matrices from a fitted lavaan object, (b) filtering out rows and columns for exogenous variables (because lavaan uses the all-y parameterization), and (c) doing the above calculation in R.

Keith

Hayduk, L. A. (1996).  LISREL:  Issues, debates, and strategies.  Baltimore:  Johns Hopkins.
Sorbom, D. (1989).  Model modification.  Psychometrika, 54: 371-383

------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.

All my latent models run properly, but when i run the same models as manifest models with mean-scores out of the same mitml.list, calculation itself seems to work, but when I want to see the results with summary(), i get the following error-message:

>   'dimnames' applied to non-array

> I'm very confused, because it sounds like a problem with a wrongly formatted list, but even if i run a model with pseudo-factors (1 indicator per factor, loading = 1, residual variance = 0) using exactly the same mean-scores as indicators, everything works properly again, gigving me again the results with summary() without such an error-message (unless there is a message that there are Heywood cases, what in my opinion could be a result of the pseudo-factors).
>
> Does anybody have an idea, what could be the problem with the manifest models?
>
>
> Thanks for all!
>
> Edgar

Edgar

Dear all,

I am trying to fit a simple linear growth model to categorical data. I have observed the log of the wage over seven different time points (1980 to 1987). I would like to compare the results obtained  using the underlying variable approach, with estimation performed using uni and bivariate information (UBN, estimator="WLSMV") as well as full information (UMN, estimator="FML").

I do not have problem in getting the UBN solution, whereas it is almost impossible to get the UMN solution based on the estimator FML. I always end up with the error message

Error in sadmvn(lower, upper, mean = MEAN, varcov = Sigma.hat, maxpts = 10000 *  :
  lower>upper integration limits

I also considered a smaller number of time points, since if I have correctly understood full information maximum likelihood under the underlying variable approach is possibile for at maximum a six-dimensional integral.

Below the syntax I wrote for both UBN and UMN:

model.0.cat <http://model.0.cat><-'
#measurement model
alpha=~1*lnwg_cat_80+1*lnwg_cat_81+1*lnwg_cat_82+1*lnwg_cat_83+1*lnwg_cat_84+1*lnwg_cat_85+1*lnwg_cat_86+1*lnwg_cat_87

I am not sure how you are planning to use the factor scores in glm() to test reliability. There are multiple reasons why I dont recommend this, like factor indeterminancy would provide bias results with only 1 set of factor scores.

Now, for the issues you are interested, you can test these with the factor analysis.
- Dimensionality: specify your theoretical model, and evaluate the factor loadings, overall, and local model fit

- composite reliability: you can use the reliability and maximalRelia functions.

messages.subject: Re: Extract a latent variable - Reliability test
messages.subject_clean: Extract a latent variable - Reliability test
messages.body_plain:
Omid

You can extract the factor scores. But because of factor indeterminancy, it is not recommended to extract only 1 set of factor scores. Factor indeterminancy means that multiple sets of factor scores can be presented as possible factor scores.

So, if you wihc to use factor scores outcise lavaan, the recommendes steps are;
1. define your factor model: here you want to describe factor loadings, etc to be able to state that the factor is "good". You can present some measures of reliability, like McDonald omega, and maximal Reliability from semTools
2. Use the plausibleValues function from semTools to extract multiple sets of factor scores (for example 100). This way you can account for variability due to factor indeterminancy. This approach has shown to reproduce the relations with the factor the best
3. Include the multiple sets of factor scores into glm(). You do this by treating the multiple sets of factor scores as multiple imputations. You could do this with the zelig package, or the with function from the mitools package
4. Use the pooled estimates from the multiple plausible factor scores as your model estimates

Hope this helps

Silvia

The first thing is that FIML does not work with categorical data. So, if you are estimating thresholds and treating your indicators as ordered categorical, you need to stick to WLSMV. Which sounds like you have no problems with it.

You could use FIML, but you would have to treat your indicators as continuous.

If you have an issue of missing data, WLS will exclude cases with any missing data, so you would need to use Multiple Imputations to handle missing data, and then run the model on the multiple imputations

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've been studying SEM, and I am trying to run the following model.

dataUse <- read.csv("SRI.cov.csv" )
covUse <- data.matrix(dataUse, rownames.force = NA)

variable_names <- paste0("Y",1:32)
Nobs <- 939

model_stepA <- '
  F1 =~ Y2 + Y3 + start(-3000)*Y4
  F2 =~ Y9 + Y11 + Y13
  F3 =~ Y14 + Y16 + Y17 + Y18 + Y19
  F4 =~ Y20 + Y21
  F5 =~ Y22 + Y23 + Y24 + Y25 + Y26
  F6 =~ Y28 + Y29

'

fit <- sem(model_stepA,
           sample.cov = covUse,
           sample.nobs = Nobs,
           std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
           )

The model has no issue in Mplus with a starting value of -3000 for Y4.

The problem is that it does not run in lavaan with the following error:

lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.

Interestingly, the estimates and fit indices are identical for Mplus and lavaan.
The only thing different is standard errors, because the information matrix isn't inverted in lavaan.

I'd appreciate any suggestions how to make lavaan compute standard errors.

Best,
Lee.

I've attached the output of Mplus for comparison.

messages.subject: Re: SEM model unable to converge when socioeconomic variables included
messages.subject_clean: SEM model unable to converge when socioeconomic variables included
messages.body_plain:
The trust variables 'trstprl', 'trstplt' and 'trstprt' are declared as
'ordered' but they have 11 levels. That leads to numerical issues,
because many pairwise combinations are empty. That is the cause of the
trouble. I have no solution yet (working on it). But I would recommend
to treat these variables as 'numeric'.

(Just out of interest, I tried Mplus on this data. That is how I learned
that Mplus stops with an error if a categorical (endogenous) variable
has more than 10 levels. That makes sense.)

Yves.

--
Yves Rosseel -- http://www.da.ugent.be
Department of Data Analysis, Ghent University

messages.subject: Re: Model running in Mplus, not running in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Model running in Mplus, not running in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
On 3/18/20 9:24 PM, Sooyong Lee wrote:
> The problem is that it does not run in lavaan with the following error:
>
> lavaan WARNING:
>      Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
>      not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
>      identified.
>
> Interestingly, the estimates and fit indices are identical for Mplus and
> lavaan.

That is already a miracle, given the bad scaling properties of your data.

> The only thing different is standard errors, because the information
> matrix isn't inverted in lavaan.

Rescale!

For example,

fit <- sem(model_stepA,
            sample.cov = covUse,
            sample.nobs = Nobs,
            std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
            )

COV <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov
D <- diag(nrow(COV))
D[3, 3] <- 1/10000 # Y4
D[5,5] <- 1/100    # Y13
D[16,16] <- 1/100  # Y24

COV.rescaled <- D %*% COV %*% D
rownames(COV.rescaled) <- colnames(COV.rescaled) <- rownames(COV)
diag(COV.rescaled)

model_stepA.bis <- '
   F1 =~ Y2 + Y3 + Y4

   F2 =~ Y9 + Y11 + Y13
   F3 =~ Y14 + Y16 + Y17 + Y18 + Y19
   F4 =~ Y20 + Y21
   F5 =~ Y22 + Y23 + Y24 + Y25 + Y26
   F6 =~ Y28 + Y29

'

fit2 <- sem(model_stepA.bis, sample.cov = COV.rescaled, sample.nobs =
Nobs, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

And this works. It is fascinating that Mplus does not blink here. I have
not found a way to handle such badly-scaled problems yet.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: lavInspect questions: Thresholds and Sigma Matrix
messages.subject_clean: lavInspect questions: Thresholds and Sigma Matrix
messages.body_plain:
> Can someone explain why the statements below do not return the same values?

>
> lavInspect(mod,what = "est")$tau

These are the estimated thresholds, interpreted relative to whatever the model-implied means/variances of latent item responses are.

> lavInspect(mod.fit,what = "th")

These are the model-implied *standardized* thresholds (i.e., interpreted relative to latent item responses that are assumed standard normal), which are merely implied by the estimated model parameters (including thresholds and variances).

When using parameterization = "delta" in models without equality constraints, these will typically be the same because the estimated thresholds are already interpreted relative to standard normal latent item responses.

> lavInspect(mod,what = "sigma")
> lavInspect(mod.fit,what = "vy")

The latter merely returns model-implied variances, which appear on the diagonal of the Sigma matrix returned by the former.

messages.subject_clean: Questions about using lavaan with multiple imputations on longitudinal data with multiple groups
messages.body_plain:
> No, we are using theta, but I couldn't come up with a reproducible example, I think it could be down to the way the latents were scaled, which differed between cfa and cfa.mi cases, will revisit this.

cfa.mi() just passes any arguments down to cfa(),  otherwise relying on its identical defaults, so that is unlikely.

> what do robust estimates mean in the context of DWLS? In ML it compensates for departures from multivariate normality, right? Do you have any literature on this topic to recommend?

DWLS fits your normal-theory model to estimated sample moments for latent responses underlying ordered observations.  So the "data" (polychoric correlations) are estimated, not known.  The robust method adjusts for this by taking uncertainty of the estimated polychorics into account.

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/1082-989X.12.1.58

> Unfortunately, I cannot install the dev version, as I get the following error when trying to run the above code (with the latest version of R):
>
> Downloading GitHub repo simsem/semTools@master
> Error: Failed to install 'semTools' from GitHub:
>   missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
>
> A colleague of mine managed to do it on her computer, so it must be some specific / weird R type bug, because it happens for other people and other packages also.

Try installing in a fresh R session, and first verify nothing has been loaded beyond the base packages

sessionInfo()

RStudio has some insidious hidden features like automatically saving workspaces and reloading them when RStudio is opened from that working directory.  This has the unfortunate side-effect of making R "remember" old crap you don't want anything to do with anymore.

> >  It could be clearer for beginners, probably, if measEq.syntax() only created syntaxes and did not actually have the ability to test models, as this could lead to confusion,

That is why the default is return.fit=FALSE.  The option was included for the eventual design of a wrapper that automates the steps to test invariance (far out on the horizon).

> 1) According to Liu, Millsap, West, Tein, Tanaka and Grimm (2017) the one threshold for each indicator in configural models should be constrained to equality across time. This is not done by the function automatically. Should we specify this by hand when supplying the configural fit object from which the specification of the configural model is derived? Or is this not necessary for scaling latents?

Read carefully  -- their advice is merely Millsap & Tein's (2004) advice applied to longitudinal data.  So you can reproduce this behavior merely by setting ID.cat="millsap"

> 2) With using the compareFit() function , what do the crosses mean next to some fit indices?

Those indicate the model preferred by each index.

> Also, the difference in chisq presented in top comparison (nested model comparison) does not equal the difference between actual chisq scaled presented in part two (model fit indices), why is this the case?

Because the robust chi-squared-difference test is not a difference between 2 robust statistics.  It applies (essentiall) the same "robustification" method to the naive chi-squared-difference statistic as is applied to the overall fit statistic.

> 3) When using the same values (thresholds and loadings) in both group.equal and long.equal, everything works fine, but when trying to keep thresholds for both the same, but constrain loadings only across groups (or across time) we get the following error:
>
> Error in GLIST.specify[[1]]$lambda[, ff] : subscript out of bounds
>
> The measEq.syntax() function should allow for different types of constraints across groups and across time, right?

Yes, and it works fine for the help-page example:

mod.cat <- ' FU1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3 + u4
             FU2 =~ u5 + u6 + u7 + u8 '
## the 2 factors are actually the same factor (FU) measured twice
longFacNames <- list(FU = c("FU1","FU2"))

measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat, data = datCat,
              ordered = paste0("u", 1:8),
              parameterization = "theta",
              ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
              group = "g", longFacNames = longFacNames,
              group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings"),
              long.equal = "thresholds")
measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat, data = datCat,
              ordered = paste0("u", 1:8),
              parameterization = "theta",
              ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
              group = "g", longFacNames = longFacNames,
              long.equal = c("thresholds","loadings"),
              group.equal = "thresholds")

> 4) With smaller models, we add some constraints to the base model ("configural") to make it identified (for example loadings across time), before suppying this fit object to the measEq.syntax(). The function later overrides this, and the configural model it outputs does not contain these constraints. In the documentation it is writen that configural.model is "A model with no measurement-invariance constraints (i.e., representing only configural invariance), unless required for model identification. ". Does this mean that they were not actually required for identification?

No, although perhaps they were required for empirical identification given your small N.  Did they not converge without those constraints?  If you need to assume additional constraints for identification, then I would recommend adding the additional identification constraints in the earliest step first.  For example, if you have categorical data on which a configural model does not converge (even after trying other methods to help it along), constrain thresholds first.  Then if that is necessary to achieve convergence, you have to consider that your least-constrained baseline model (in place of a configural model).

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> to perform multi group analysis and show groups are different, is there any assumption about sample sizes ? should all groups have almost the same sample sizes or not?

No assumption in the unrestricted model (freely estimate the correlation in each group).  If you fit a model constraining it to equality across groups, the estimate will be most driven by the largest group's data, because there is more of it.  But that doesn't cause a problem if you only use the restricted model to conduct a LRT of the equal-correlations null hypothesis (i.e., just don't interpret the "pooled estimate" as though it were actually an unweighted average across 3 countries).

> personally, I think it is not fair and groups should be equal, but on the other hand, I can see that Swiss is much smaller than France so I can not expect having the same sample size as France.

If you want to interpret a pooled correlation from a constrained model, then it sounds like sampling weights should be used so that your results would reflect an average based on actual population sizes of those countries.

Well, it technically does, but only with estimator = "MML", which is currently disabled in lavaan (experimental functionality needs more development).

> thank you so much. FML is not the FIML estimator, in the sense that it has been developed to perform full information maximum likelihood for models with categorical data based on the underlying variable approach.
> It should work, but got stuck with the error in the sadmv function that is used to perform numerical integration.

FML is not an option:

?lavOptions # see "estimator"

Another option is pairwise ML, which can be used in combination with pairwise deletion to utilize all available information (like FIML does when maximizing the likelihood of the entire set of variables).

data(datCat, package = "semTools")
lapply(datCat, class)
## impose missing values
set.seed(123)
for (i in 1:8) datCat[sample(1:nrow(datCat), size = .1*nrow(datCat)), i] <- NA

cfa(' f =~ 1*u1 + 1*u2 + 1*u3 + 1*u4 ', data = datCat,
    estimator = "PML", missing = "pairwise")

messages.subject: Re: How can I get residual correlations for a nonrecursive model with both continuous and binary endogenous variables?
messages.subject_clean: How can I get residual correlations for a nonrecursive model with both continuous and binary endogenous variables?
messages.body_plain:
> Could you perhaps clarify what the following labels are indicating, when running nonrecursive models with both continuous and binary endogenous variables (diagonally weighted least squares):
>
>
> $res.cov, $res.int <http://res.int/>, $res.th <http://res.th/>, $res.slopes, $cov.x, $mean.x
>

Nothing to do with nonrecursive models.  By default, lavaan partials out exogenous effects when estimating polychoric correlations, to assuage the computational instabilities involved with DWLS.  Thus, your model is fitted to the residual polychorics, intercepts, etc., given the exogenous variables in your model.

res.slopes contains the exogenous effects, and cov.x & mean.x are the sample moments of the exogenous variables.

> Are both $res.cov and $res.slopes what I am looking at to assess standardized residual correlations (those greater than 0.1 warranting closer attention)?

Not necessarily.  The interpretation of residuals gets very complicated, especially if your hypothesized model does not estimate all possible effects of exogenous variables on each of the endogenous variables.  To get back to familiar territory, you could simply set conditional.x=FALSE and interpret the usual standardized residuals.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> That is exactly what I was expecting but I am getting results different from that.

OK, turns out for categorical data, "vy" is the model-implied variances of the latent item responses (not necessarily 1), whereas "sigma" will return the model-implied polychoric correlations (i.e., the diagonal will be 1s).  See below when using theta parameterization.

## make binary items
HS9 <- HolzingerSwineford1939[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5",
                                 "x6","x7","x8","x9")]
HSbinary <- as.data.frame( lapply(HS9, cut, 2, labels=FALSE) )

## fit 3-indicator CFA
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HSbinary, ordered=names(HSbinary),
           parameterization = "theta")

## these don't match
lavInspect(fit, "sigma")
lavInspect(fit, "vy")

## but the variances match the standard expectation for covariance structure
EST <- lavInspect(fit, "est")
LAMBDA <- EST$lambda
PSI <- EST$psi
THETA <- EST$theta
LAMBDA %*% PSI %*% t(LAMBDA) + THETA

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
Ina,
  I am not sure that I fully understand your model specification.  So, I could easily be missing something.  However, here are some tentative thoughts.

1. Check the distribution of your binary outcome variable.  If b0 is on a standard scale, then the value 3.853 would suggest very little variability.

2. Consider whether you could have a scaling issue such that an effect of .00005 is a very large effect.  If so, consider whether you can adjust the scaling to move the effect parameters into a more easily represented range of values.  (Of course, re-scaling will not impact the confidence interval including zero.)

3. Given that parameter a is negative (although it seems odd that the estimate is on the boundary of the confidence interval), consider whether it is possible that you have a case of an unfaithful covariance matrix because the direct effect cancels out the indirect effect.

4. Check your degrees of freedom.  Also check your degrees of freedom if you run the model with fixed.x = FALSE.  I am probably just missing something but it is not clear to me why your model has non-negative degrees of freedom.  (You seem to be getting reasonable standard errors though, judging from the confidence intervals.  I am unclear why they did not print.  However, I tried a simplified version of your model and did not obtain standard errors.  So, there is something that I am not reproducing accurately form what you posted.)

5. Consider whether you have any other outcome variables, even uninteresting ones, that could be added to the model.  If I understand correctly, your mediator measurement model is identified by the outcome acting as an additional indicator, and a binary outcome with possibly low variance may not be offering much information.

6. Consider whether you need to saturate the covariances between the indicators.  Consider whether it might be worth trying the model without these covariances, or without some of them.

Keith

Since my input data is binary, I am trying to define the mean and var of the LIR so that threshold can be correctly calculated LIR ~ N(0,1) as per your presentation.

My goal is to expand the current transversal model (time1) to create a longitudinal mode (with time 2). Goal is to estimate how the latent mean changes in time having the LIR fixed at N(0,1) in time 1.

I do not understand why setting

int1==0
int2==0
int3==0

instead of

int1+int2+int3==0
int1 + l1*lv1mean ==0

int2 + l2*lv1mean ==0
int3 + l3*lv1mean ==0

gives me the following warnings. It seems to suggest that the means equation is not identified.

> In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
>   lavaan WARNING:
>     The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
>     does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue

>     (= 4.511264e-18) is close to zero. This may be a symptom that the
>     model is not identified.
>

(in which the conditional rather than marginal variances are constrained to 1)

Yes, I noticed i have mislabeled my models. Thank you.

Hugo

--------------------------------------------

 rm(list=ls())

if(!require(MASS)) install.packages("MASS"); library(MASS)
if(!require(rockchalk)) install.packages("rockchalk"); library(rockchalk)
if(!require(lavaan)) install.packages("lavaan"); library(lavaan)

if(!require(mirt)) install.packages("mirt"); library(mirt)

# Generate Longitudinal Items from a Bivariate LIR
data_creation <-function(){}

N <- 2000 ## subjects
I= 3  # Number of Items
PL=2 # Logistic Model (1,2,3 parameters)
SigmaType <- 3 # 0 = Covariance Uniform, 1 = Covariancia AR1, 2 =  Covariancia de bandas 3 = Covariancia Nula
rho<-0.7

coefs <- matrix(ncol=6,nrow=I)
colnames(coefs)=c("a1","b1","c1","a2","b2","c2")

if (PL==1) {a = rep(1,I)} else {a = runif(I,0.5, 2.5)}    # U(0.5 , 2.5)
b = runif(I,-2, 2.0)     # U(-2 , 2)
if (PL<=2) {c = rep(0,I)} else{c = runif(I,0.0, 0.3) } # U(0 , 0.3)

d=-a*b # MIRT trabalha com o intercepto (d=-ab) e nao com a dificuldade (b)

if(SigmaType==0){
  Sigma <- lazyCor(c(rho,rho,rho)) #Matriz de Covariancia Uniforme
}else if(SigmaType==1){
  Sigma <- lazyCor(c(rho,rho*rho,rho)) #Matriz de Covariancia AR(1)
}else if(SigmaType==2){
  Sigma <- lazyCor(c(rho,0,0)) #Matriz de Covariancia de bandas
}else if(SigmaType==3){
  Sigma <- lazyCor(c(0,0,0)) #Matriz de Covariancia nula
}else{
  Sigma <- NULL
}
Sigma

Theta <- mvrnorm(n=N, mu=c(0,0.5,1), Sigma )

dat =simdata(a=a,d=d,N=N,itemtype = '2PL', Theta = matrix(Theta[,3],ncol=1,nrow = length(Theta[,1])))

colnames(dat) <-    c("y2w1","y2w2","y2w3")

prop <- colSums(dat)/nrow(dat)
th <- qnorm(1-prop)
th #expected thresholds

mod2ind3lv1.indicator_effects.delta_marginal <- '

lv1 =~ l1*y2w1 + l2*y2w2 + l3*y2w3
l1 + l2 + l3 == 3

lv1 ~ lv1mean*1
lv1 ~~ lv1var*lv1

## LIR means
y2w1 ~ int1*1
y2w2 ~ int2*1
y2w3 ~ int3*1
int1+int2+int3==0

int1 + l1*lv1mean ==0 #<- new constraint
int2 + l2*lv1mean ==0 #<- new constraint
int3 + l3*lv1mean ==0 #<- new constraint

## thresholds link LIRs to observed items
y2w1 | thr1*t1
y2w2 | thr2*t1
y2w3 | thr3*t1

## LIR (co)variances
 y2w1 ~~ var1*y2w1 + 0*y2w2 + 0*y2w3     # problematic lines
 y2w2 ~~ var2*y2w2 + 0*y2w3                     # problematic lines
 y2w3 ~~ var3*y2w3                                     # problematic lines

lv1var*l1^2 + var1 == 1 # delta parameterization <- new constraint
lv1var*l2^2 + var2 == 1 # delta parameterization <- new constraint
lv1var*l3^2 + var3 == 1 # delta parameterization <- new constraint

'

mod2ind3lv1.indicator_effects.theta_conditional <- '

lv1 =~ l1*y2w1 + l2*y2w2 + l3*y2w3
l1 + l2 + l3 == 3

lv1 ~ lv1mean*1
lv1 ~~ lv1var*lv1

## LIR means
y2w1 ~ int1*1
y2w2 ~ int2*1
y2w3 ~ int3*1
int1+int2+int3==0
int1 + l1*lv1mean ==0

int2 + l2*lv1mean ==0
int3 + l3*lv1mean ==0

# int1==0
# int2==0
# int3==0

## thresholds link LIRs to observed items
y2w1 | thr1*t1
y2w2 | thr2*t1
y2w3 | thr3*t1

## LIR (co)variances
y2w1 ~~ var1*y2w1 + 0*y2w2 + 0*y2w3     # problematic lines
y2w2 ~~ var2*y2w2 + 0*y2w3                     # problematic lines
y2w3 ~~ var3*y2w3                                     # problematic lines

var1==1 #theta parameterization

var2==1 #theta parameterization
var3==1 #theta parameterization

'
theta <-TRUE
if(theta==TRUE){
  sem.model <- mod2ind3lv1.indicator_effects.theta_conditional
  param = "theta"
}else{
  sem.model <- mod2ind3lv1.indicator_effects.delta_marginal
  param = "delta"

}

rm(mod2ind3lv1.fit)
mod2ind3lv1.fit <- lavaan(model = sem.model,
                          data = dat,
                          std.lv <http://std.lv> = FALSE,
                          int.ov.free = TRUE,
                          int.lv.free = FALSE,
                          meanstructure =TRUE,
                          auto.fix.first = FALSE,
                          auto.var = TRUE,
                          auto.th <http://auto.th> = TRUE,
                          ordered = c("y2w1","y2w2","y2w3"),

                          parameterization = param)

summary(mod2ind3lv1.fit)
fitMeasures(mod2ind3lv1.fit)[c("df",'tli',"cfi","rmsea")]

lavInspect(mod2ind3lv1.fit,what = "est")$tau

lavInspect(mod2ind3lv1.fit,what = "vy")

qnorm(1-prop[2],mean = lavInspect(mod2ind3lv1.fit,what = "mu")[2], sd = sqrt(lavInspect(mod2ind3lv1.fit,what = "vy")[2]))

messages.body_plain:
Omid

I dont think you need to test the reliability with other methods. With categorical indicators, the use of the polychoric correlation adjusts for the type of item. So there are no unnecesary assumptions about the items.

The mayor difference in direction between measures (omega = 0.08, MR = 0.6), I would think is due to having at least one factor loadings being negative, and others being positive. Alpga dn omega need all the items to be in the same direction, while MR does not. If I am right, if you reverse code the item(s) that are negative you should have an omega that makes more sense

Between reliability measures I recommend omega3 and Maximal Reliability, instead of alpha, as alpha has many issues and these 2 are better methods accounting by the SEM model

Cho, E., & Kim, S. (2015). Cronbach’s Coefficient Alpha: Well Known but Poorly Understood. Organizational Research Methods, 18(2), 207–230. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428114555994
Gu, F., Little, T. D., & Kingston, N. M. (2013). Misestimation of Reliability Using Coefficient Alpha and Structural Equation Modeling When Assumptions of Tau -Equivalence and Uncorrelated Errors Are Violated. Methodology, 9(1), 30–40. https://doi.org/10.1027/1614-2241/a000052

messages.body_plain:
Omid

I hate these cutoff values, because they are arbitrary and have NO technical criteria to defend them. These come from Nunnally, which said: based on our experience 0.7 is a good overall guideline. It was never suggested as a strong cutoff. This 0,7 comes from alpha, and have have been extended to omega, again with no technical criteria

This has become such a common practice, that have lead to people fudging the data until they reach that score. As well as choose the measures that "look" better. Like in your case, how alpha looks a lot better than omega and MR. But we know that alpha its a biased measured, as it assumes tau equivalence, and this has shown that can be either higher or lower biased (Raykov, dont have the exact year). While omega and MR doesnt assume tau equivalence.

It has become really easy to calculate alpha and report it as passing this 0.7 score. Which has lead to the common practice to report "reliability" with little to no thought about validity.

For more details about these issues

Cho, E., & Kim, S. (2015). Cronbach’s Coefficient Alpha: Well Known but Poorly Understood. Organizational Research Methods, 18(2), 207–230. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428114555994

Now, to your commet about "should you use this factor?". This is a more complex questions than just saying "is reliability higher than the arbitrary cutoff?". You should be looking at factor loadings, does the overall model makes sense and present strong relations? Could be that the factor loadings are not strong enough?

You can describe omega and MR as the continuous interpretation, instead of the good/bad binary based on the cutoff: proportion of true score variance based on variance explained by the factor

Also, there are other factors that could be having an effect, for example number of items, most of these measures will report higher scores with more items. And in your example you have a only 3 items

I agree that the value of 0.58 feels low. But my overall point is that the issue is much more complicated that higher/lower than 0.7

messages.body_plain:
Hi Omid and Mauricio
If I can, I'd like to add a little to what the meaning of scale reliability is.
Cattell (back in 1964; how quickly we forget) made it clear that there was a conceptual distinction between reliability and homogeneity of items in a set. What he meant is that if you have items that are highly homogeneous (i.e., the say almost the same thing with the same words) then reliability will be high--he called it a bloated specific. I'm sure you can think of some high reliability scales that achieve that by redundant repetition of item wording.
So if your scale items are not homogeneous but describe the latent construct well, I would expect low reliability estimates but good fit to the data from a confirmatory factor analysis of a latent structure. Perhaps this is what you have ended up in? low reliability because items are heterogeneous but acceptable or good fit to the data?
see
Cattell, R. B. (1964). Validity and reliability: A proposed more basic set of concepts. Journal of Educational Psychology, 55(1), 1-22.
Cattell, R. B., & Tsujioka, B. (1964). The importance of factor-trueness and validity, versus homogeneity and orthogonality, in test scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 24(1), 3-30.

messages.body_plain:
> Could you please let me know whether the approach to Model 2 is correct and/or how you would approach this?

I don't see anything necessarily wrong with your syntax, but I notice your model syntax regresses Y on X, yet your path diagram excludes that effect.  Was that intentional?  FYI, your user-defined "total effect" would include more indirect effects if you also meant to model (e.g.) direct effects of X on M2, or of M1 or Z on Y, which are also excluded from the diagram.

If Z is binary, you could perhaps simplify your specification and interpretation by using Z as a grouping variable to define a multigroup model.  You can then easily allow for Z to moderate all effects by virtue of estimating parameters separately in each group (Z=0 and Z=1).  You would label parameters unique for each group, and define your indirect effect of interest separately per group, making it easy to define "index" essentially the same way, as the difference between indirect effects in groups 0 and 1.

messages.body_plain:
> I am trying to define the mean and var of the LIR so that threshold can be correctly calculated LIR ~ N(0,1) as per your presentation.

Then why are you trying to estimate the common-factor mean?  It is ultimately an arbitrary location, so it is much simpler if you just let it remain fixed to zero for identification.  That way, the conditional LIR means (i.e., intercepts) are already interpreted as the means when the common-factor == its mean (because it is zero).  Then you don't need to break your back trying to correctly define the parameters needed for your identification constraints; lavaan's default constraints will already do that (assuming you use cfa() or set the same lavOptions that cfa() does).

When you get to your longitudinal model, you simply need to specify invariance constraints across time, which allow the common-factor mean to be estimated at Time 2.  Because the common-factor's mean at Time 1 is fixed to zero, the Time-2 mean can already be interpreted as the change from Time 1.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Omid,
  Three observations...

1. I completely agree with the spirit of the comments from Mauricio and Gavin.  However, the .7 benchmark (not really accurate to call it a cut off) actually has an interesting basis.  The benchmarks of .7 for a new test and .9 for an established test (people tend to forget that .7 is only for new tests still in development) are based on the standard error of measurement.  Reliability of .7 roughly corresponds to a standard error of measurement of .5 and .9 roughly corresponds to .3.  I do not bring this up to justify reviewer behavior making radically different interpretations of .69 and .70.  That is nonsense.  However, I have found that it is a real eye opener for students when I show them how inaccurate a scale with reliability of .7 is in terms of standard error of measurement.

2. The basic concept behind reliability is that each observations contains error but the errors cancel out over large numbers of observations.  So, the very idea of estimating reliability for a three-item scale is a little dodgy.  Evaluating the reliability of a 3-item scale is a little like estimating a population mean from a sample of 3 observations.  You can go through the motions but you are pressing the limits of the underlying assumptions.  Expecting long-run properties to kick in at N=3 is a big ask.  (I am a little confused how you got down to only 3 items.  Are these three scale scores computed form more items?  If so, parceling may not be your friend in this context.)

3. I did not have time to pursue this earlier but it is not clear to me why you want to extract factor score estimates for use in a predictive model.  It is not clear to me why you could not use lavaan's probit link to model the dichotomous outcome in the same model as the measurement parameters.  I may have missed something in your description.

messages.body_plain:
Omid,

  >>> Lavaan does not support interactions between independent and the latent construct.

  I do not understand what you mean by that.  I think that 'independent' means an exogenous observed variable.  It is true that the LISREL all-y model underlying lavaan does not directly represent effects involving observed variables.  However, path analysis and other models involving such effects are readily incorporated using single-indicator latent variables.  Once you have a single-indicator latent variable, you can proceed as you would with a multiple-indicator latent variable.  You can then use methods for interactions between latent variables.  I could imagine that a very large number of interactions could lead to a very complex model that might swamp your sample size.  You would probably want to build up the model one term at a time or possibly write a program to write the lavaan model syntax if the model is very complicated.  However, unless I am misunderstanding something, I believe that the model is expressible in lavaan model syntax.

  PS:  I realized after I sent my last post that I should have made it explicit that I was referring to standard errors of measurement expressed in standard deviation terms.

messages.subject: Re: system of equations, discrete time, time lagged
messages.subject_clean: system of equations, discrete time, time lagged
messages.body_plain:
Andy,
  To obtain a linear representation, I think that you need to first multiply though.  For simplicity, to avoid commas, I write X1t1 and X1t2 where time 2 comes after time1.  I am also assuming that the sign of the parameter is arbitrary so that I can treat -parameter(variable) as parameter(variable).

(1) X1t2 = (X1t1) + (a1 * X1t1) + (b1 * X1t1^2) + (v1 * X1t1 * X4t1)

Now, the first two terms can be expressed as follows.

(2) (X1t1) + (a1 * X1t1) = (1 + a1) * X1t1

So, you might as well simplify by letting a1 represent the original a1 + 1.  That allows you to eliminate the first term.

(3) X1t2 = (a1 * X1t1) + (b1 * X1t1^2) + (v1 * X1t1 * X4t1)

  This assumes that your data is in wide format and you write an equation for each variable at each time.  This in turn assumes that the time points are comparable for all cases.  You would need to augment your data set with polynomial and product terms.  After you estimate the transformed parameters, you could subtract 1 or multiply by  -1 to obtain your original parameters.

Keith

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence Jorgensen,

Thank you very much for your helpful reply.

So to clarify, do I set conditional.x=FALSE and manually specify covariances and variances among my exogenous variables, in order to get residual correlations with the "residuals(fit.model, type = "cor")" command?

I want to be able to see if any of my residual correlations exceed the absolute value of 0.1 to get an idea of how good the "local fit" is. Would I get residual correlations only when I set conditional.x=FALSE and do not specify anything else among my exogenous variables?

Also, can residual correlations be obtained with the diagonally-weighted least squares? Or is it only possible with maximum likelihood estimation?

Thank you very much!

On Saturday, March 21, 2020 at 11:41:37 AM UTC-4, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Could you perhaps clarify what the following labels are indicating, when running nonrecursive models with both continuous and binary endogenous variables (diagonally weighted least squares):
> >
> >
> > $res.cov, $res.int <http://res.int/>, $res.th <http://res.th/>, $res.slopes, $cov.x, $mean.x
> >
>
> Nothing to do with nonrecursive models.  By default, lavaan partials out exogenous effects when estimating polychoric correlations, to assuage the computational instabilities involved with DWLS.  Thus, your model is fitted to the residual polychorics, intercepts, etc., given the exogenous variables in your model.
>
> res.slopes contains the exogenous effects, and cov.x & mean.x are the sample moments of the exogenous variables.
>
> > Are both $res.cov and $res.slopes what I am looking at to assess standardized residual correlations (those greater than 0.1 warranting closer attention)?
>
> Not necessarily.  The interpretation of residuals gets very complicated, especially if your hypothesized model does not estimate all possible effects of exogenous variables on each of the endogenous variables.  To get back to familiar territory, you could simply set conditional.x=FALSE and interpret the usual standardized residuals.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

Also to consider, "normal" SEM is not great for long time series data. If you have multiple variables for a lot of time points other approaches would be better. Like

1. LDE: latent differential equations, re-structure the data and growcth curve model parameterization to approximate derivatives for dynamic models. This can be done in lavaan
2. Continuous time SEM: look at continuous change over time (dynamic models), independent of the lag time between measurements. This cannot be done in lavaan, you can use the ctsem package
3. state space modeling: can estimate discrete tine and continuous time dynamic models. lavaan cannot do this, you can use the package dyner

hope this helps

messages.body_plain:
Dear Yves Rosseel,
I am at the same "dead end" at the moment. I'd like too include a manifest, exogenous variable to correlate it with my latent variables and I am wondering if you could find a solution for this restriction?

Thank you in advance and best wishes,
Ann-Kathrin

Am Donnerstag, 19. Februar 2015 17:42:40 UTC+1 schrieb Yves Rosseel:
> On 02/18/2015 05:32 PM, Pahud wrote:
> > no, I don't get a warning msg or errmsg. No msg at all.
> > If I model my manifest variable direct into the model, without modelling
> > it as a latent variable first, it just doesn't work... no msg or
> > anything like it.
> >
> > Let me put it different: Why do we model a single manifest variable into
> > a latent variable first, before we're able to cor. it with a latent
> > variable?
>
> Ah, ok. I now understand what you mean. And you are right: this is
> currently a restriction of lavaan: if you have exogenous observed
> variables, they can only enter the model in the right-hand side of a
> regression formula. Not in a covariance formula.
>
> The workaround, as you have found yourself, is to 'upgrade' this
> covariate to a latent variable (with a single indicator).
>
> I will see if I can make this happen automatically in a next update. At
> the very least, a warning would have been appropriate.
>
> Yves.

I want to run the regression with 21 control (independent) variables which include country dummies. Lavaan does not support interactions between independent and the latent construct. I was thinking maybe I could do that in probit regressions using glm(). Maybe treating the extracted factor estimates as an independent continuous variable in regression using glm() function and setting up interactions with it is fully wrong and I don't know this.
> >

> > > Omid,
> > >   Three observations...
> > >
> > > 1. I completely agree with the spirit of the comments from Mauricio and Gavin.  However, the .7 benchmark (not really accurate to call it a cut off) actually has an interesting basis.  The benchmarks of .7 for a new test and .9 for an established test (people tend to forget that .7 is only for new tests still in development) are based on the standard error of measurement.  Reliability of .7 roughly corresponds to a standard error of measurement of .5 and .9 roughly corresponds to .3.  I do not bring this up to justify reviewer behavior making radically different interpretations of .69 and .70.  That is nonsense.  However, I have found that it is a real eye opener for students when I show them how inaccurate a scale with reliability of .7 is in terms of standard error of measurement.
> > >
> > > 2. The basic concept behind reliability is that each observations contains error but the errors cancel out over large numbers of observations.  So, the very idea of estimating reliability for a three-item scale is a little dodgy.  Evaluating the reliability of a 3-item scale is a little like estimating a population mean from a sample of 3 observations.  You can go through the motions but you are pressing the limits of the underlying assumptions.  Expecting long-run properties to kick in at N=3 is a big ask.  (I am a little confused how you got down to only 3 items.  Are these three scale scores computed form more items?  If so, parceling may not be your friend in this context.)
> > >
> > > 3. I did not have time to pursue this earlier but it is not clear to me why you want to extract factor score estimates for use in a predictive model.  It is not clear to me why you could not use lavaan's probit link to model the dichotomous outcome in the same model as the measurement parameters.  I may have missed something in your description.

messages.subject: Re: How to integrate a single manifest variable proberly into my SEM?
messages.subject_clean: How to integrate a single manifest variable proberly into my SEM?
messages.body_plain:
Ann-Kathrin,
  Why are you at a dead end?  Does the preceding thread not describe how to do what you want to do?  Here is a simple example.

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example (modified)
HS.model <- '
    visual  =~ 1*x1 + x2 + x3  # Latent variable
    visual ~~ visual
    x1 ~~ x1
    x2 ~~ x2
    x3 ~~ x3

    age =~ 1*ageyr             # Observed variable
    ageyr ~~ 0*ageyr
    age ~~ age

    age ~~ visual              # Covariance between the two
' # end HS.model

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)

Keith

messages.body_plain:
You have not shared your model syntax, so I can't give guidance reating to your specific model's structure.
So what do you know about that group's data? You are treating the variables as ordinal--look at two-way crosstabs within that group. You want to see a pattern suggesting the correlations that you expect. Look at the correlation matrix for that group. (Yes, you are treating teh data as ordinal, but you are just looking for a clue about what is wrong.) Check for outliers or data entry errors within that group. If some variable were a constant within that group, lavaan would have said so. But maybe there is a perfect collinearity within that group, or maybe a lack of variation that lavaan did not signal.

messages.body_plain:
Ugur,
  I believe your are correct about the logit link.  This is not something that I do every day, so hopefully I have not missed anything.  Here is a simple example.

summary(HolzingerSwineford1939)

# simplified mediation model
babyModel <- '
  school ~ x1 + x2
  x1 ~ x2
  school~~school
  x1~~x1
  school | t1
  x1 ~ 1
' # end babyModel

# Examine and Fit model
lavaanify(babyModel)
babyFit <- lavaan(babyModel, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, ordered=c('school'))
summary(babyFit)

# Extract coefficients from model fit
babyCoef <- coef(babyFit)
# Choose a set a values for the predictor
plotX2 <- seq(from=0, to=9, len=100)
# Predict mediator values
plotX1 <- babyCoef[6] + babyCoef[3]*plotX2
# Predict latent continuous outcome values
plotSchoolZ <- babyCoef[1]*plotX1 + babyCoef[2]*plotX2
# predict probabilities
plotSchoolP <- pnorm(plotSchoolZ)

# Draw plot
plot(x=plotX2, y=plotSchoolP, type='l', lwd=2, xlab='Mediated Predictor',
  ylab='Predicted Probability of Outcome', main='Predicted Probability Plot')

Keith

On Mar 27, 2020, at 1:35 PM, Edward Rigdon < edward.rigdon <http://edward.rigdon>@gmail.com <http://gmail.com>> wrote:

﻿
You have not shared your model syntax, so I can't give guidance reating to your specific model's structure.
So what do you know about that group's data? You are treating the variables as ordinal--look at two-way crosstabs within that group. You want to see a pattern suggesting the correlations that you expect. Look at the correlation matrix for that group. (Yes, you are treating teh data as ordinal, but you are just looking for a clue about what is wrong.) Check for outliers or data entry errors within that group. If some variable were a constant within that group, lavaan would have said so. But maybe there is a perfect collinearity within that group, or maybe a lack of variation that lavaan did not signal.

messages.subject: Re: Moderated Mediation-Probit link, computing conditional simple and indirect effects & plotting
messages.subject_clean: Moderated Mediation-Probit link, computing conditional simple and indirect effects & plotting
messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

I hope you are well! I ran the moderated mediation model below and the interaction term (mediator and moderator both continuous, and ideation is binary) was significant.
I need to probe and plot the significant probit-link interaction. I read up on computing marginal effects  <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/margins/vignettes/TechnicalDetails.pdf>to accurately interpret the non-linear interaction term. The 'margins' R package has been helpful, but I would prefer to extract the coefficients directly from the output yielded by the code below. (The margins package suggests I run a probit-link lm or glm for the b paths not accounting for the a path). I would like to ask for your help in using lavaan to run and plot predicted fitted values and  estimated marginal effects for the probit-link interaction effect. Would you be able to help me get started on that effort?

modmediation14 <-

# a path

Isolation_c~ a1*Violence_c

# b paths

Ideation~ cp*Violence_c
>
> + b1*Isolation_c #mediator
>
> + b2*Support_c #moderator 1SDbelow =-1.025341, 1SDabove = 1.025341
>
> + b3*IsolationXSupport #interaction term

# Covariances

Violence_c ~~Violence_c +
>
> + Support_c +
> + IsolationXSupport
>

Support_c~~Support_c +
> IsolationXSupport

IsolationXSupport~~IsolationXSupport

Ideation~~Ideation

# Intercepts

Violence_c~1

Isolation_c ~1

IsolationXSupport~1

ideation ~1

ideation|0*t1

# index of moderated mediation

a1b3 := a1*b3

# test conditional indirect effects #

mod.belowmean  := a1*b1 + (a1b3 * -1.025341)

mod.atmean        := a1*b1 + (a1b3 * 0)

mod.abovemean := a1*b1 + (a1b3 * 1.025341)

# test conditional total effects #

total.belowmean := cp + (a1*b1) + (a1b3 * -1.025341)

total.atmean        := cp + (a1*b1)

total.abovemean := cp + (a1*b1) + (a1b3 * 1.025341)

# proportion mediated #

pro.belowmean := a1*b1 + (a1b3 * -1.025341)/cp + (a1*b1) + (a1b3 * -1.025341)

pro.atmean       := a1*b1 + (a1b3 * 0)/cp + (a1*b1)

pro.bovemean  := a1*b1 + (a1b3 * 1.025341)/cp + (a1*b1) + (a1b3 * 1.025341)

'

# fit model

fit14=lavaan(modmediation14, data=data1, ordered=c('Ideation'), estimator='DWLS', se = 'bootstrap', bootstrap=10000L,  link = "probit", fixed.x=FALSE, auto.var = TRUE, meanstructure=TRUE)

--

On Sun, Dec 15, 2019 at 5:27 AM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > I updated the code (in blue font) to compute the conditional effects/simple slopes of the significant interaction term of the probit regression.
>
> Your code in the first post was correct.  The blue font you added does not make sense.  The effect of a moderator is not conditional on itself (that would be a quadratic effect).
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Rookie question here -- but how does one interpret betas in lavaan output when the indicators of the latent variables have different scales? The whole “for every one unit increase in x the value of y increases by _” of standard regression doesn’t really work here. I imagine that this is part of why you need to set the scale (so the latent variable will be based on the scale of the indicator you assign), but still don't know how final coefficients are interpreted. I feel like there's probably a simple answer I'm just missing. Thank you!

Best,

Kimberley
